articles.excerpt: This article was originally published in Japanese on Zenn. Hi, I'm Kohei Matsunobe, a second-year student in the online (correspondence) program at ZEN University. I'm working toward becoming an AI en…
articles.body: This article was originally published in Japanese on Zenn . Introduction Hi, I'm Kohei Matsunobe, a second-year student in the online (correspondence) program at ZEN University. I'm working toward becoming an AI engineer, and on my own I run experiment pipelines that evaluate LLM outputs and code on notebooks and cloud runtimes. GPU runtimes are great, but they're expensive per hour, and there's a cap on how many compute units you can use. I've made the same mistakes more than once: "I grabbed a GPU, launched the real job, and it crashed in the first few minutes," or "it crashed, I didn't notice, and the runtime just sat there running." Looking back, almost all of those failures could have been caught without a GPU.
articles.author: kohei matsunobu

articles.title: Summarize Kaggle Notebook Status and Logs in ~7 Lines with the Kaggle CLI (Goodbye, .bat + Notepad)
articles.excerpt: This article was originally published in Japanese on Qiita. Hi, I'm Kohei Matsunobe. I'm a second-year student in the online (correspondence) program at ZEN University, studying to become an AI engine…
articles.body: This article was originally published in Japanese on Qiita . Introduction Hi, I'm Kohei Matsunobe. I'm a second-year student in the online (correspondence) program at ZEN University, studying to become an AI engineer. Once I started running Kaggle notebooks (kernels) from my local machine with kaggle kernels push , one small thing kept eating my time: checking what was going on. Is it still running? Did it finish? Did it fail? And if it failed, where? Checking that in the browser or digging through log files every single time got old fast. In this post, I'll share a script that calls kaggle kernels status and kaggle kernels output from Python and boils the status and log down to a ~7-line summary plus one CSV row .

articles.title: One hotel API vs ten supplier integrations: what we learned
articles.excerpt: From the TraveleXe engineering team. We build APINex, a unified travel API — this post is about the trade-offs, including when you shouldn't use one. If you're building a travel booking product, you'l…
articles.body: From the TraveleXe engineering team. We build APINex, a unified travel API — this post is about the trade-offs, including when you shouldn't use one. If you're building a travel booking product, you'll hit the supplier question early: integrate each hotel supplier directly, or put one aggregation layer in front of all of them? Direct integrations give you full control of each supplier's features and no middle layer. The cost: every supplier has its own schema, auth, error codes, rate-limit behaviour and certification process. Ten suppliers is ten of everything, and they all change on their own schedules. A unified API gives you one schema, one auth model and normalised responses.
articles.author: Travelexe edge91

articles.body: Haq (حق) — Making Legal Information Accessible with Local AI This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 4: Ghost in the Machine . What I Built I built Haq Guide (حق گائیڈ) , a privacy-focused legal information assistant designed to help people understand their rights, legal notices, agreements, and available options in plain language. The idea behind Haq is simple: legal information shouldn't be difficult to access or understand. Users can describe their situation or upload a legal document, such as a notice or agreement. Haq helps break down the information, identify important details, explain relevant rights and options, and point users towards official resources and legal aid.

articles.title: My API Was Returning Every User's Password Hash. I Didn't Notice for Weeks.
articles.excerpt: Why a FastAPI endpoint happily sends back fields you never meant to expose, and the one line that filters them out. The endpoint looked harmless. Fetch a user, return the user. @app.get("/users/{user_…
articles.body: Why a FastAPI endpoint happily sends back fields you never meant to expose, and the one line that filters them out. The endpoint looked harmless. Fetch a user, return the user. @app.get ( " /users/{user_id} " ) async def get_user ( user_id : int ): user = await db . get_user ( user_id ) return user It worked. It returned the user's name, email, everything the frontend needed. Nobody looked twice. Weeks later, someone opened the browser network tab while debugging an unrelated issue and went quiet. The JSON response for that endpoint had a field none of us wanted anyone to see. { "id" : 42 , "username" : "anna" , "email" : "anna@example.com" , "password_hash" : "$2b$12$Q9...." , "is_admin" : true , "internal_notes" : "flagged for review" } The password hash. The admin flag.

articles.body: If your agent can reach the internet, hold a long-lived key and write its own logs, it doesn't need to "go rogue" to cause an incident. It just needs a task and an open door. That's the practical reading of this year's agent incidents. OpenAI's technical report says agents in a July 2026 cyber evaluation, run with certain safeguards disabled, exploited a flaw in an internal package-mirror service to reach the internet. They then used publicly exposed credentials, together with vulnerabilities in Hugging Face's own infrastructure, to compromise parts of its production systems.

articles.body: Our time on our "space mission" underwater was coming to an end, and I felt like what I imagine an astronaut on the International Space Station (ISS) must feel before returning to Earth. On one hand, you are excited to return to your home and loved ones, as well as to fresh food and normal hygiene. On the other, you know you will miss your crew and the incredible experience of being in space. We did this to live and work like astronauts on the ISS .

articles.excerpt: Asked about supply chain shortages, like the ongoing RAM shortage, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman said in an interview that it's "terrible" to have RAM in personal PCs instead of data centers. During his appea…
articles.body: Asked about supply chain shortages, like the ongoing RAM shortage , OpenAI CEO Sam Altman said in an interview that it's "terrible" to have RAM in personal PCs instead of data centers. articles.title: India launches next-gen navigation satellite to orbit (video)
articles.excerpt: India launched the NVS-03 navigation satellite to orbit today (Oct. 30) atop a GSLV rocket. It was the fourth orbital launch from Indian soil so far this year.
articles.body: India bolstered its homegrown satellite-navigation system today (Oct. 30). A GSLV Mark II rocket launched the nation's NVS-03 satellite from Satish Dhawan Space Centre today at 2:21 p.m. EDT (1821 GMT and 11:51 p.m. India Standard Time). Everything went well: The rocket deployed NVS-03 into geostationary transfer orbit as planned, officials with the Indian Space Research Organisation (ISRO) announced on X about 30 minutes after liftoff. An Indian GSLV Mark II rocket launches the NVS-03 navigation satellite on Oct. 30, 2026. (Image credit: ISRO) NVS-03 is the third next-gen satellite that India has launched for the Navigation with Indian Constellation (NavIC), its version of the United States' Global Positioning System ( GPS ).

articles.title: 5 horror franchises that went to space... and one that absolutely should have but didn't
articles.excerpt: In space, no one can hear you scream, a bit like the empty theater screens that some horror franchise's final installments limp. But there are still some real gems among the space-based frightfests.
articles.body: In space, no one can hear you scream... not unlike in the empty theater screens that aging horror franchises play to when the lustre has gone and their final installments limp to the public. It is perhaps little wonder that some horror franchises go to space to die... or take long breaks, at least. In celebration of Halloween , we're running down some horror franchises that made the journey to the final frontier, resulting in films that range from the sublime and outrageously campy fun to just pure awful. Absent from the list are space horror movies that have space baked into their natural fabric. So no Event Horizon, no Alien, and no Critters 4 (they were aliens, so they just went back to space; that doesn't count). 1.
